title: Automate resume screens
description: A system that scores resumes against your criteria, then reruns blinded to catch bias before anyone acts on the ranking.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

slack.title: Slack
slack.content: The team messaging app most companies run on. In Level 2, students connect Slack to their AI tools to trigger workflows from messages, post AI-generated updates to channels, or summarize threads automatically.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

batch-api.title: Batch API
batch-api.content: A way to send a big pile of requests to Claude at once and get the results back later (usually within 24 hours) at a discount. Good for one-time bulk jobs like classifying 10,000 customer support tickets.

read-only.title: Read-only
read-only.content: The first rung of the trust gradient: the agent can see your inbox, calendar, or docs but can't change anything. The default starting state for every new tool connection. Tiny blast radius, fast to ship, and confirms the read side works before you graduate the write side.

automation.title: Automation
automation.content: Having Claude run tasks automatically on a schedule or trigger — without you manually starting them each time. For example, checking your inbox every morning and summarizing it to Slack.

children.text: 62% of employers now use AI in talent acquisition, up from 40% in 2020, and screening resumes is the second most common use case among them at 44%, per [SHRM's Recruiting Executives Priorities and Perspectives 2026](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/research/recruiting-executives-priorities-perspectives-2026/repp26-full-report). This system scores every resume in a [batch](#tooltip-batch-api) against your must-have and nice-to-have criteria, then runs a second pass with names, schools, and locations stripped out to check whether the scores move.

Most teams that use AI in hiring only apply it to a sliver of the process, per [Aptitude Research's AI Adoption in Talent Acquisition](https://www.aptituderesearch.com/ai-adoption-in-talent-acquisition-why-62-of-companies-use-ai-but-true-adoption-still-lags/). A homemade screener can itself count as a regulated automated employment decision tool in some jurisdictions, which is why the bias check runs as a gated step on every batch. The output is a ranked shortlist plus a bias delta a person has to read and explain before anyone acts on it.

Run it as a paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) for each requisition, a saved [skill](#tooltip-skill), or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that watches a resume inbox. Every version stays [read-only](#tooltip-read-only) against your ATS.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a scope naming the role you hire for most, your must-have and nice-to-have criteria, where resumes land, and what would make you distrust a score.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that screens resumes against a job description and checks itself for bias before I trust its output. Ask me questions, one at a time, about the role I hire for most often, what my must-have vs nice-to-have criteria actually are, where resumes land today (email, ATS export, a folder), and what would make me distrust a score. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview forces you to write down criteria you've been applying by instinct, and the scope document becomes the brief every screening batch gets measured against.

items: Where resumes land (an ATS export, a shared inbox, a folder someone forwards you).
Whether your company already has a legal or compliance sign-off process this needs to route through.
Whether the role sits in a jurisdiction with its own audit or disclosure rule.

children.text: Bring the scope document and gather your ATS (Greenhouse, Lever, Workday), your resume inbox (Gmail, a shared drive folder), and your HR or legal team's review process ([Slack](#tooltip-slack), email). The paste-in version needs none.

**Create.** Start building the system your scope document describes, and test it on the job description and a real batch of resumes. The prompt below is an example. Your scope document will give you a version shaped to your setup.

children.prompt:
Goal: Score every resume in [folder/ATS export] against the job description for [role name], then re-run the same scoring with names, schools, and locations stripped out and flag any candidate whose rank shifts.

Context: Job description is at [path/link]. Must-have criteria: [list]. Nice-to-have: [list]. Resumes are in [format: PDF/plain text].

Rules:
- Score 1-5 on each must-have with one sentence of evidence per score.
- Never infer age, gender, or ethnicity from a name or school.
- Flag any resume you can't confidently score instead of guessing.
- Output a ranked table plus a separate bias check table showing blinded vs unblinded rank for every candidate.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: scoring the same batch twice with identity details stripped turns bias into a number you can see, instead of a hunch.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Evidence on every score, no inferred demographics, blinded ranks next to unblinded ones?
**Feedback.** Tell it what went wrong ("this nice-to-have is outweighing a must-have, fix the tiebreak") and fold each correction into the rules.

items: Extend the bias check into a full blind-screening pipeline that never shows names until after scoring.
Add a skills-extraction pass that pulls structured skills data instead of matching keywords.
Add a fact-check pass that catches inflated or hallucinated qualifications in AI-written candidate summaries.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric). Have your AI chat draft the rubric and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each screening pass, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, role, candidates screened, bias deltas flagged, and flags overturned after review. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and the log columns make a pattern of rank-shifting criteria visible after a few hiring cycles.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Note the date, what passed or failed, and what changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from the log. Once the rubric passes a few runs straight, package the prompt and corrected rules into a reusable AI skill. A check that keeps failing is your next candidate. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s skill-creator skill interviews you and writes it, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).

One failure mode. A screener that looks objective can still encode bias from the criteria you gave it as much as from the resumes it reads. Never let a score replace a human decision without a visible reason.
